findings.summary: TD Bank, N.A. and TD Bank USA, N.A. entered a coordinated U.S. BSA/AML resolution: FinCEN imposed a $1.3 billion civil money penalty, the OCC assessed $450 million and imposed a cease-and-desist order with an asset cap/growth and business restrictions, and the Federal Reserve fined parent Toronto-Dominion Bank $123.5 million; TD reported total payments of approximately US$3.09 billion across the OCC, Federal Reserve, FinCEN and DOJ. TD Bank, N.A. agreed to plead guilty to a criminal violation of 18 U.S.C. §371 and TD Bank US Holding Company to criminal violations of 31 U.S.C. §§5322 and 5324, with approximately $1.89 billion payable to DOJ; the DOJ filing described repeated AML transaction-monitoring deficiencies, and the resolution requires remediation and independent compliance review.

The CFPB ordered TD Bank to pay $7.76 million in consumer redress and a $20 million civil money penalty for repeatedly furnishing inaccurate negative information to consumer reporting companies, including systemic errors concerning credit-card delinquencies and bankruptcies.

The CFTC ordered The Toronto Dominion Bank (TD Bank), a swap dealer, to pay a US$75 million civil monetary penalty, cease and desist, and undertake remediation for recordkeeping and supervision failures involving firm-wide use of unapproved communication methods, including personal text messages; TD Bank admitted the facts in the order.

The CFTC ordered The Toronto Dominion Bank (TD Bank) to pay a $4 million civil monetary penalty and cease and desist over supervision failures that caused it not to surveil certain communications for hundreds of swap-dealer personnel over a five-year period; TD Bank admitted the facts and acknowledged violations of the Commodity Exchange Act and CFTC regulations.

In 2024, U.S. regulators imposed US$3.09 billion in monetary penalties on TD Bank's U.S. subsidiaries, along with business restrictions and an asset cap on TD Bank's U.S. retail banking growth. TD was reported to have pleaded guilty to multiple charges related to AML-program failures, and its subsidiaries to conspiracy to commit money laundering.

Shareholder class-action proceedings alleged that The Toronto-Dominion Bank and certain directors and officers misrepresented the effectiveness of its AML controls and related investigations. On November 3, 2026, Justice Janet Leiper granted leave and certified the Ontario misrepresentation class action against TD and senior leaders, including former CEO Bharat Masrani; the plaintiffs allege a CA$30 billion market-capitalization loss, and the defendants deny the allegations.

On October 13, 2026, Judge Arun Subramanian of the Southern District of New York partially denied the defendants' motion to dismiss Tiessen v. The Toronto-Dominion Bank, allowing the securities fraud class action to proceed to discovery. The amended complaint alleges misrepresentations about TD's Bank Secrecy Act and AML controls, including that senior management knew of long-term, systemic deficiencies.

A proposed class action was filed with the Ontario Superior Court of Justice on July 8, 2026 against Toronto Dominion Bank and TD Securities Inc., with Calvin Wong as the proposed representative plaintiff. It alleges that the defendants failed for years to pay required vacation and holiday pay on employees' incentive and other pay under their employee incentive programs.

Trisal v. TD Bank, N.A., filed on October 2, 2025, alleged that TD Bank unlawfully assessed unrefunded $35 overdraft fees even when customers cured overdrafts by the following business day. Federal court records listed the grace-period suit as terminated on May 15, 2026.

On June 27, 2025, Judge Renee Marie Bumb of the New Jersey federal court dismissed a proposed class action alleging that TD Bank wrongfully shared customers' personal financial information through Meta's Pixel tracking code. The court found insufficient allegations of standing and concrete harm and dismissed all claims, but allowed plaintiff Jefferey Stevens to amend his complaint.

In In re TD Bank / First Horizon Securities Litigation in the District of New Jersey, lead plaintiffs filed a third amended complaint on January 31, 2025 on behalf of First Horizon securities purchasers. The action concerns alleged misrepresentations about TD Bank's BSA/AML compliance and proposed First Horizon acquisition, which the source says regulators refused to approve because of TD Bank's concealed AML deficiencies; a defense motion to dismiss was due March 14, 2025.

The Burns v. TD Bank, N.A. class action challenged APSN overdraft fees assessed when transactions were authorized with a positive available balance but later paid with insufficient funds. TD Bank denied wrongdoing, but a $32,225,000 settlement received final approval on October 15, 2024, with payments beginning in March 2025.

On February 15, 2024, the Ontario Superior Court of Justice approved a settlement in the Canadian duplicative NSF-fee class action against The Toronto-Dominion Bank and The Canada Trust Company. The class covered personal deposit account holders charged an NSF fee on a re-presented pre-authorized debit transaction between February 2, 2019 and November 27, 2023.

TD Bank, N.A. pleaded guilty on October 10, 2024 to conspiring to fail to maintain a BSA-compliant anti-money-laundering program, fail to file accurate currency transaction reports, and launder monetary instruments; its parent, TD Bank US Holding Company, simultaneously pleaded guilty to related charges. TD Bank agreed to pay US$1.8 billion to resolve the DOJ investigation, FinCEN assessed a record US$1.3 billion penalty, and the coordinated DOJ, FinCEN, OCC and Federal Reserve resolutions brought total penalties to almost US$3.1 billion.

TD Bank insider Wilfredo Aquino pleaded guilty to conspiring to launder monetary instruments. While a TD Bank assistant store manager, he facilitated a network that moved approximately US$474 million through TD Bank accounts and accepted retail gift cards totaling over US$11,000.

Nunez, then a TD Bank employee in Scotch Plains, New Jersey, pleaded guilty to conspiring to launder monetary instruments and receipt of bribes by a bank employee. He accepted bribes to open shell-company accounts and issue debit cards used to facilitate the transfer of over US$26 million from the United States to Colombia.

Former TD Bank employee Leonardo Ayala pleaded guilty to conspiring to launder monetary instruments and receipt of bribes by a bank employee. He opened fraudulent accounts and issued or unblocked debit cards used to funnel approximately US$5.5 million to Colombia, receiving more than US$6,000 in bribes.

Former TD Bank employee Gerardo Aquino pleaded guilty to conspiring to launder monetary instruments and receipt of bribes by a bank employee for accepting bribes and laundering more than US$4.8 million to Colombia while employed by TD Bank.

OFAC announced a $115,005.04 settlement with TD Bank, N.A. for apparent violations of the North Korea Sanctions Regulations and the Foreign Narcotics Kingpin Sanctions Regulations. TD Bank processed 1,479 transactions totaling $382,685.38 and maintained nine accounts for employees of North Korea’s UN mission without an OFAC license, and separately maintained accounts for an SDN-listed U.S. resident and allowed $35,514.13 in transactions by that person; the apparent violations were voluntarily self-disclosed and non-egregious.

Thieves stole thousands from Stephen and Tessa Savage's TD Bank accounts through Zelle and online banking after ransomware targeted their home computer. TD Bank twice denied the couple's Regulation E refund request, stating once that there was no error and once that the transfers were authorized.

A breach at TD Bank partner NCB Management Services began on February 1, 2023 and was detected on February 4, affecting more than 1 million individuals, primarily TD Bank customers. Names, Social Security numbers, account and card details were exposed and listed on the dark web, prompting class actions and regulatory scrutiny.

TD Bank disclosed in February 2025 that a former employee had unauthorized access to customer information between August and December 2022, affecting at least eight Massachusetts residents; the employee was terminated and TD worked with law enforcement. Coverage of the confirmed breach said names, contact details, account numbers and, in some cases, Social Security numbers were exposed, TD offered identity protection, and a class action alleging negligence and inadequate data security remained active, with litigation reported as progressing in 2025.

TD reported to Massachusetts regulators on June 15, 2026 that an employee had unauthorized access to U.S. customer records from January 7 to January 30, 2026. The insider incident potentially exposed names, addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth, Social Security numbers, account numbers and transactional data; no external hacking or further misuse was reported at disclosure.

TD Bank disclosed to Massachusetts regulators on September 15, 2026 a data security event that may have exposed customer personal and financial information; 54 Massachusetts residents were identified, while the nationwide total was not disclosed. Potentially exposed data included Social Security numbers, government-issued identification, pay stubs, W-2 forms, financial account information and payment-card numbers, and TD offered two years of Fraud-Defender identity monitoring.

The CFPB ordered TD Bank to pay $28 million for years of inaccurate consumer-credit reporting, including information it knew or suspected was fraudulent, and for failing to properly investigate disputes, affecting hundreds of thousands of customers. CFPB Director Rohit Chopra criticized TD Bank management for prioritizing growth and mergers over fixing the problems.

A Senate letter on TD Bank’s DOJ resolution, which included a historic $3 billion fine, said bank leadership knowingly presided over a criminally deficient anti-money-laundering program and high-level executives knew of serious problems, yet DOJ did not charge them and structured the charges to shift legal liability to holding company TD BHC. Commentary on the plea agreement and consent order said senior management repeatedly ignored warnings and speculated, without confirmation, that one or more whistleblowers may have helped build the government’s case.
